title: Latency per Dollar Benchmark Report — Draft Outline (v0.6)
body:
Doc purpose
- Working outline for the public-facing benchmark report (PDF + web). This doc is not final copy.
- Includes: section headers, narrative intent, chart inventory, and open questions for reviewers.
- Owner: Ethan. Primary reviewers: Soojin (messaging), Claire/Jonas/Sana (methodology & variance language), Nadia (cost/metering), Michael Grant (claims/legal), Elliot/Wei (docs/web packaging).

Audience
- Primary: engineers + ML engineers evaluating inference providers or self-hosting.
- Secondary: platform/procurement/security stakeholders who need defensible methodology and predictable unit economics.

Core narrative (single sentence)
- “Latency per dollar is the production metric that ties user experience to cost; Redwood makes it measurable and actionable across models and regions.”

Proposed report title options (pick 1)
1) “Latency per Dollar: A Production Economics Benchmark for LLM Inference (2025)”
2) “Production Economics Benchmarks: Latency/$ Across Models and Regions (2025)”
3) “The Latency/$ Report: Measuring Real-World LLM Inference Economics (2025)”

One-liner for press/landing (draft)
- “A reproducible benchmark that compares latency per dollar across popular open models and cloud regions, with variance bands and methodology you can audit.”

Disclaimer/claims guardrails (must appear early)
- Results are specific to: disclosed workloads, regions, request distributions, time window, and Redwood serving configuration.
- We report variance / confidence bands and describe rerun policy.
- No claim of universal best performance; highlight tradeoffs and applicability.

Report structure (proposed)

0) Cover + report metadata
- Title, date/month, version (v1.0), authorship line.
- “What’s inside” bullets (2–3).
- QR / link to landing page.

1) Executive summary (1–2 pages)
Goal
- Quickly communicate: what latency/$ is, why it matters, what we measured, and the top takeaways.

Key elements
- 3 headline findings (non-superlative framing).
- What’s included (models/regions/workloads) and what’s not.
- “How to use this report” (choose your model/region based on constraints).

Draft headline takeaways (placeholders; final numbers from public table build)
- Takeaway A: “Across regions, latency/$ varies meaningfully even when raw latency looks similar — cost is the differentiator.”
- Takeaway B: “At moderate concurrency, batching behavior becomes a first-order driver of latency/$.”
- Takeaway C: “Some model families have stable latency/$ across regions; others show higher variance (capacity/price differences).”

CTA (end of exec summary)
- “Run a free trial (Hosted API)”
- “Talk to us about Dedicated/Private capacity”
- “Reproduce a subset of the benchmark on your workload” (link to example repo/docs)

2) Why “latency per dollar” (concept section)
Goal
- Explain metric in plain engineering terms; make it defensible.

Content notes
- Define: latency (p50/p95), throughput (tok/s), and cost per 1M tokens.
- Define latency/$ precisely (see methodology) and why it’s a useful combined metric.
- Show a simple example: two deployments with same p95 latency but different cost; which is better and why.
- Include: “Latency/$ is not a substitute for quality; quality is held constant by pinning model versions.”

Potential sidebar
- “If you only optimize for $/token, you can degrade UX; if you only optimize for latency, you can overspend. Latency/$ forces the tradeoff into one number.”

3) Methodology overview (non-technical summary)
Goal
- Build trust without overwhelming. Detailed appendix later.

Must include
- Workloads measured (chat + embeddings baseline) and why selected.
- Regions measured (list) + measurement window.
- Hardware class disclosure level (TBD: how specific we can be publicly without creating security/capacity risk).
- Concurrency settings and request distribution (sequence length / output length distributions).
- Warmup policy, caching policy, batching policy, and consistent runtime flags.
- Rerun/variance policy and what triggers a rerun.

Tone
- “Here’s what we controlled and why.” Avoid “we tuned for best results.”

4) Benchmark results (core pages)
Goal
- Make results scannable and credible; allow readers to zoom into model family + region.

Organization proposal
Option A (recommended): results by workload → region → model family
- 4.1 Chat results (all regions overview)
- 4.2 Chat results (region pages)
- 4.3 Embeddings results (all regions overview)
- 4.4 Embeddings results (region pages)

Option B: results by region first → workload → model family
- Better for region-minded buyers (EU/APAC). Check with Lukas/EMEA feedback.

Result page template (repeats)
- Top chart: Latency/$ comparison (with variance bands)
- Supporting: p50/p95 latency, cost/1M tokens, throughput
- “Interpretation” bullets (2–4)
- “If you care about X, choose Y” guidance (careful not to be prescriptive beyond data)
- Footnote: run config + time window + model versions.

5) Interpreting the results (how to apply)
Goal
- Provide practical guidance; reduce misinterpretation.

Topics
- Variance and confidence: what it means, what it doesn’t.
- Why region differences happen (pricing, capacity, routing, network).
- When your results may differ (prompt mix, longer contexts, tool calling overhead, multi-turn patterns, safety filters, etc.).
- How to choose model + region based on constraints (latency SLO, budget, residency, reliability).

6) Reproduce a subset (developer appendix-lite)
Goal
- Give engineers a concrete path; avoid “black box benchmark” critique.

Content
- Link to reproduction example.
- Minimal steps: select region header, pin model version, run baseline script, compare metrics.
- “What we recommend you change for your workload” (prompt distribution, concurrency).

7) Redwood product tie-in (1–2 pages)
Goal
- Translate benchmark credibility into product value without turning report into a brochure.

Must connect to report themes
- “Unified inference across hosted/dedicated/private deployments” (same API, same operational tooling).
- Cost/performance levers: batching/caching/quantization profiles + routing policies.
- Observability: token-level cost + latency dashboards.

Include
- Short callouts: Hosted API, Dedicated, Private
- CTA block at end with links

8) Appendix A — Full methodology (technical)
Goal
- Make it auditable.

Outline
- A1. Definitions and formulas (latency/$, cost attribution)
- A2. Workload definitions + prompt sets (high level; no proprietary prompts if sensitive)
- A3. Request distributions (tables)
- A4. Concurrency model + measurement windows
- A5. Runtime settings (caching/batching) + justification
- A6. Data quality / filtering rules (timeouts, failed requests)
- A7. Variance analysis + rerun policy
- A8. Limitations

9) Appendix B — Model/region coverage matrix
- Table of all included model families and regions.
- “Inclusion criteria” + planned refresh cadence.

10) Appendix C — Glossary
- tok/s, TTFT (if included), p50/p95, KV cache, batching, quantization.

11) Appendix D — Security & data handling (short)
- “No customer data, no customer traces; benchmark traffic is synthetic/test prompts.”
- What telemetry is collected and retained (high level).

Chart inventory (draft)

Global charts (appear in exec summary + results sections)
C1. “Latency/$ by model family (overall) — Chat”
- Chart type: bar chart or dot plot with error bars
- X: latency/$ (units must be consistent + explained)
- Y: model families
- Series: regions (color-coded) OR separate small multiples per region

C2. “Latency/$ by model family (overall) — Embeddings”
- Similar to C1

C3. “Cost per 1M tokens vs p95 latency (bubble chart) — Chat”
- X: cost/1M tokens
- Y: p95 latency
- Bubble size: throughput (tok/s) or requests/min at target concurrency
- Color: model family
- Purpose: show tradeoff space; avoids a single-number argument

C4. “Variance bands / run-to-run stability”
- Chart type: error bars or violin plot (depending on design)
- Purpose: show we measured variance + rerun rules

Per-region charts (repeatable page template)
C5. “Region spotlight: latency/$ ranking table (top N + full table link)”
- Table: model, p50 latency, p95 latency, tok/s, cost/1M, latency/$, notes

C6. “TTFT vs steady-state token latency (optional; if we have clean data)”
- Only include if we can support it rigorously across models

Methodology charts (appendix)
C7. “Request distribution (input/output lengths) — Chat”
- Histograms or percentile table

C8. “Concurrency sweep (selected model) — how latency/$ changes with load”
- Purpose: show that workload matters; reduce cherry-pick critique

Chart decisions needed (design + methodology)
- Do we include TTFT publicly? (Pros: dev relevance. Cons: easy to misinterpret; more variance.)
- Do we show absolute numbers for all metrics or only relative ranking + tables? (Credibility vs noise)
- How we show error bars: 95% CI vs min/max vs p10/p90 across runs (Sana to advise)

Tables (public + report)
T1. Coverage matrix (models x regions)
T2. Definitions table (metrics + units)
T3. Public results table excerpt (top rows) + link to full downloadable CSV/JSON

Narrative notes (draft copy guidance)
- Keep tone “here’s what we measured” vs “we won.”
- Use consistent language: “observed,” “measured,” “in our benchmark,” “within this methodology.”
- Always pair a ranking statement with a constraint statement.
- Add “What changed since last run” only if we commit to refresh cadence; otherwise omit.

Landing page alignment (notes)
- PDF report is the deep asset; landing page should:
  - Lead with 1 sentence definition + 3 bullets of what’s included
  - Provide interactive table (if approved) or at minimum a filterable table snippet
  - Include FAQ: methodology, variance, data handling
  - CTAs: Hosted API signup, book consult, reproduce guide

Open questions for reviewers (please comment inline)
1) Models: which families are “must include” for credibility vs time? (Need final list locked for charts.)
2) Regions: final APAC region selection + naming convention (e.g., “Tokyo” vs “APAC-Northeast”).
3) Metric definition: do we publish the exact formula for latency/$ in the report body or only in appendix?
4) Variance language: do we state “confidence intervals” or “run-to-run variability bands” (legal/methodology preference)?
5) Unit clarity: should latency/$ be expressed as “ms per $” or “tokens per $ at p95 latency target” (readability vs precision)?
6) Hardware disclosure: what level is acceptable publicly (GPU family yes/no)?
7) Caching/batching: what do we say about defaults to avoid “benchmark tuned” accusations while staying transparent?
8) Comparison framing: do we avoid naming competitors entirely, or include “industry context” without vendor claims?
9) Data residency: add a dedicated EU callout page? (Requested by Lukas/EMEA thread.)
10) Reproduction: can we safely publish a minimal prompt set without exposing internal eval IP?

Next steps (as of last edit)
- Ethan: incorporate methodology summary language from Claire/Jonas + claims guardrails from performance standards.
- Soojin: review exec summary headline framing (no over-claims).
- Sana: recommend variance visualization + wording.
- Nadia: confirm cost/1M token derivation disclosure (metering validation).
- Tessa/Alicia: propose chart style direction + page templates for PDF.
- Elliot/Wei: align appendix placement and link strategy for docs site.

Change log
- v0.4 (2025-02-03): added chart inventory + variance section; added reproduce section.
- v0.5 (2025-02-07): reorganized results by workload; added EU residency open question.
- v0.6 (2025-02-10): added security/data handling appendix + clarified claims guardrails.
